# Angiostatin

**Angiostatin** is an endogenous anti-angiogenic protein fragment generated by proteolytic cleavage of [[Plasminogen]]. It is one of the most potent naturally occurring inhibitors of [[Angiogenesis]], suppressing endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and survival. Angiostatin is primarily generated by matrix metalloproteinases—most notably [[MMP-12]]—and plays a critical role in the balance between pro- and anti-angiogenic signalling in tissue remodelling, wound healing, and cancer.

## Structure & Generation

- **Precursor:** Angiostatin is derived from [[Plasminogen]] (92 kDa), a circulating serine protease zymogen. Plasminogen contains five kringle domains (K1–5) connected by disulfide bonds, followed by a serine protease domain.
- **Active fragments:** The most studied angiostatin forms contain kringle domains K1–3 (angiostatin K1–3, ~38 kDa) or K1–4 (~45 kDa). Kringle 5 is also anti-angiogenic but less potent. The kringle domains are responsible for anti-angiogenic activity; the protease domain is not required.
- **Generators:**
  - **MMP-12:** The most efficient generator of angiostatin from plasminogen. MMP-12 cleaves at specific sites within the kringle domain boundaries, releasing K1–3 and K1–4 fragments.
  - **MMP-3:** Stromelysin-1 can generate angiostatin by cleaving plasminogen.
  - **MMP-7:** Matrilysin generates angiostatin in intestinal epithelium.
  - **MMP-9:** Gelatinase B generates angiostatin in certain contexts.
  - **Other proteases:** Neutrophil elastase, cathepsin D, and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) can also cleave plasminogen to generate angiostatin-like fragments.
- **Regulation:** Angiostatin generation is regulated by the balance between MMPs and their inhibitors ([[TIMP1]], [[TIMP3]]), and by the availability of plasminogen at the site of cleavage.

> [!important] MMP-12 as the Primary Generator
> [[MMP-12]] is the most potent MMP for generating angiostatin from plasminogen. This positions MMP-12 as a dual-function enzyme: pro-inflammatory (via chemokine processing) yet anti-angiogenic (via angiostatin generation), with context-dependent roles in cancer and tissue remodelling.

## Mechanism of Action

Angiostatin inhibits angiogenesis through multiple mechanisms:

- **Endothelial cell apoptosis:** Angiostatin induces apoptosis of proliferating endothelial cells by binding to cell-surface receptors, including ATP synthase (ATP5B) and angiomotin, activating pro-apoptotic signalling pathways.
- **Inhibition of endothelial migration:** Angiostatin blocks endothelial cell migration by interfering with integrin-mediated adhesion and focal adhesion kinase (FAK) signalling.
- **Suppression of proliferation:** Angiostatin inhibits endothelial cell proliferation by suppressing ERK1/2 and Akt signalling downstream of VEGF and FGF-2 receptors.
- **Disruption of mitochondrial function:** Angiostatin binds to ATP synthase on the endothelial cell surface, disrupting mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP production, contributing to growth arrest and apoptosis.

## Physiological Roles

### Wound Healing & Tissue Remodelling
Angiostatin generation helps regulate the switch from the angiogenic phase (new vessel formation) to the resolution phase of wound healing. By limiting excessive neovascularization, angiostatin contributes to vascular stabilisation and tissue maturation.

### Immune Surveillance
By modulating angiogenesis in inflammatory tissues, angiostatin helps control immune cell trafficking and oedema formation. Excessive angiostatin generation may impair immune cell delivery to sites of infection.

### Pregnancy
The angiostatin/plasminogen balance is modulated during pregnancy to regulate uterine angiogenesis and placental vascularisation.

## Role in Cancer

Angiostatin has a primarily **anti-tumorigenic** role in cancer biology:

- **Tumour dormancy:** Primary tumours can generate angiostatin that suppresses the growth of distant micrometastases, contributing to tumour dormancy. Surgical removal of the primary tumour may eliminate the angiostatin source, allowing metastases to grow ("angiogenic switch").
- **Anti-angiogenic therapy:** Recombinant angiostatin and angiostatin-derived peptides have been tested in clinical trials as anti-angiogenic cancer therapies, though results have been mixed.
- **Dual role of MMP-12:** MMP-12 generates angiostatin (anti-tumorigenic) but also processes chemokines that promote tumour angiogenesis (pro-tumorigenic), illustrating the context-dependent nature of MMP-12 in cancer.

> [!tip] Therapeutic Potential
> Angiostatin-based therapies aim to starve tumours of their blood supply. While recombinant angiostatin showed promise in preclinical models, clinical trial results have been disappointing, possibly due to insufficient dosing, tumour escape mechanisms, or the dual pro-/anti-angiogenic roles of the generating proteases.

## Pathological Relevance

- **Cancer:** Elevated angiostatin levels correlate with tumour dormancy and better prognosis in some cancer types. Loss of the primary tumour (surgery) can release metastases from angiostatin-mediated suppression.
- **Retinal diseases:** Dysregulated angiostatin contributes to pathological retinal angiogenesis when the angiostatin/VEGF balance is disrupted.
- **Atherosclerosis:** Angiostatin may modulate intraplaque angiogenesis, influencing plaque stability.

## Connections

  - [[MMP-12]]: Primary generator of angiostatin from plasminogen; MMP-12's anti-angiogenic function opposes its pro-angiogenic chemokine-processing activity
  - [[Plasminogen]]: Precursor substrate from which angiostatin is proteolytically cleaved
  - [[Angiogenesis]]: Angiostatin is a potent endogenous inhibitor of pathological angiogenesis
  - [[MMP-3]]: Stromelysin-1 can generate angiostatin from plasminogen
  - [[MMP-9]]: Gelatinase B generates angiostatin in certain contexts
  - [[Cancer]]: Angiostatin suppresses tumour angiogenesis and contributes to tumour dormancy
  - [[TIMP1]]: Inhibits MMPs that generate angiostatin; the TIMP/MMP balance regulates angiostatin production
  - [[VEGF]]: Pro-angiogenic counterpart; the VEGF/angiostatin balance determines angiogenic switch
  - [[Endostatin]]: Fellow anti-angiogenic fragment; endostatin is derived from collagen XVIII, angiostatin from plasminogen
